<b>1785</b>Charles-Augustin de Coulomb p: 1785Charles-Augustin de Coulomb publishes that the force between two charges falls with the square of the distance. From that law comes a potential that falls as 1/r, the same one found on the ground around a fallen cable.
<b>1827</b>Georg Simon Ohm publica que l: 1827Georg Simon Ohm publishes that the current through a conductor is proportional to the voltage across its ends: V = I·R. With it we calculate the current that flows through the body.
<b>Siglo XX</b>Charles Dalziel, en la Un: 20th centuryCharles Dalziel, at the University of California, Berkeley, measures in volunteers which currents can be endured and for how long. From his data come the step and touch voltages allowed by the earthing standards for substations.
<b>2014</b>En España, el Reglamento de i: 2014In Spain, the Regulation on high-voltage electrical installations (RD 337/2014) requires in its ITC-RAT 13 that earthing systems keep step and touch voltages below certain safe limits.
El suelo homogéneo que conduce la corrie: Homogeneous ground that conducts current behaves, mathematically, like a vacuum with a charge: the current I entering at the contact point takes the place of the charge and the resistivity ρ, that of 1/ε. The potential is that of a point charge, and the step voltage is the potential difference between the two feet.
Se abre con una carga puntual de 1,77 µC: It opens with a point charge of 1.77 µC (which satisfies k·q = ρI/2π = 15.9 kV·m) in SI. We get a potential difference of 8.0 kV between the feet at 1 m and 2 m from the contact, 145 V between 10 m and 11 m, and a field of 15.9 kV/m at 1 m.

Un cable caído en el campo: A fallen cable in the countryside

Una tormenta tumba un poste y el cable d: A storm knocks down a pole and the high-voltage cable falls to the ground without coming off the line. This is what is called an earth fault: the cable is still live and all its current looks for a path to the earth.\n\nIt seems nothing is happening, but someone approaching on foot is about to step into an electric field that cannot be seen. The same happens next to a tree struck by lightning or the earthing of a substation.
La corriente se reparte por el suelo: The current spreads through the ground
es la densidad de corriente a una distan: is the current density at a distance r from the contact point.
El suelo no es un aislante: conduce, aun: The ground is not an insulator: it conducts, although poorly. The current entering at a point spreads in all directions, like growing hemispheres.\n\nAt a distance $r$ all the current crosses a hemisphere of area $2πr^2$, so the current density is $J = {I}/{2πr^2}$. The further away, the more spread out and weaker: at 1 m it is $J = 159 "A/m"^2$ and at 10 m, only $1.6 "A/m"^2$.
El potencial baja al alejarte: The potential falls as you move away
respecto de un punto muy lejano, junto a: relative to a very distant point, next to the fallen cable.
Para que la corriente avance por el suel:
For the current to advance through the ground a field $E = ρJ$ is needed, and the ground near the cable is at a higher potential than the distant one. Integrating from $r$ to infinity:

$V(r) = {ρ I}/{2π r}$

With $ρ = 100 "Ω·m"$ (damp clay) and $I = 1000 "A"$ we get $V = 15.9 "kV·m"/r$: 15.9 kV at 1 m, 8.0 kV at 2 m, 1.6 kV at 10 m. It is the same formula as the potential of a point charge, with ρI/2π in place of $kq$.
entre un pie a 1 m del cable y el otro a: between one foot 1 m from the cable and the other 2 m.
Si andas, tus pies pisan puntos del suel:
When you walk, your feet step on points of the ground at different potentials. With one foot 1 m from the cable and the other 2 m, a step of 1 m:

$ΔV = V(1) − V(2) = 15.9 − 8.0 ≈ 8 "kV"$

That is the step voltage. It is greater the closer you are (the potential falls very quickly near the cable) and the longer your stride. At 10 m it is already $ΔV = V(10) − V(11) ≈ 145 "V"$.
through the body with one foot at 1 m: deadly. At 10 m, about 90 mA.
Tus piernas, de pie a pie, son una resis:
Your legs, from foot to foot, are a resistance of about $1000 "Ω"$, and each foot in contact with the ground adds $3ρ = 300 "Ω"$. In total $R = 1000 + 2 · 300 = 1600 "Ω"$.

The current is $I = ΔV/R$: at 1 m, $8 "kV"/1600 "Ω" ≈ 5 "A"$; at 10 m, $145 "V"/1600 "Ω" ≈ 90 "mA"$; at 20 m, about 24 mA. From about 30 mA breathing can stop, and between 50 and 100 mA, the heart fibrillates.

The current from foot to foot does not pass through the heart, but the muscles contract, you fall and then the path already crosses the chest.
Cómo salir: pies juntos: How to get out: feet together
si los dos pies están al mismo potencial: if both feet are at the same potential, no current passes from one to the other.
La tensión de paso depende de la distanc: The step voltage depends on the distance between the feet, so the solution is to bring them together. If both feet step at the same time on points at the same distance from the cable, they are at the same potential and no current passes through the legs.\n\nIf you find yourself in such an area, stand still with your feet together or move away by hopping with your feet together, or taking penguin steps, very short, without lifting one foot past the other. And warn others not to come near. Four-legged animals suffer more: their legs are further apart and the current crosses their chest.
